title: Backspace String Compare
description: Brute force to optimized: a stack-based typing simulation versus an O(1)-space backward walk with a pending-cancellation skip counter.

blocks.text: Given two strings s and t, return true if they are equal when both are typed into empty text editors, where the character '#' represents a backspace (deleting the previously typed character, if any).

blocks.caption: A stack directly simulates typing: regular characters push, and "#" pops (deletes) the most recently typed character

blocks.text: Each string must be "typed out" character by character, where a regular letter appends to the current text, and a "#" deletes the most recently typed character (doing nothing if the text is currently empty); the two final results are then compared for equality.

blocks.title: Analogy: Comparing Two People's Typing, Including Their Typos and Corrections
blocks.text: Imagine two people each typing out a message, where pressing the backspace key deletes whatever they just typed. Even if their KEYSTROKES look completely different (one might type more, make more typos, and backspace more), what matters is only what actually ends up on the screen at the end. A stack naturally captures "what's currently on the screen," since backspacing simply removes the topmost (most recent) character.

blocks.caption: Regular characters are pushed onto the stack; a "#" pops the most recently pushed character, exactly like a real backspace key

blocks.text: The most direct approach is to simulate typing each string separately (using a stack, since backspacing removes the MOST RECENT character), then simply compare the two final results.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A regular character always gets appended to whatever is currently typed.

Observation 2: A "#" removes the MOST RECENTLY typed character, exactly matching a stack's pop operation, and safely does nothing if nothing has been typed yet.

Observation 3: Since each string is processed completely independently, building each one's final result separately (using its own stack) and then comparing them directly answers the question.

Observation 4: A further optimization exists (walking BOTH strings from their ends simultaneously, skipping backspaced characters on the fly) that avoids needing O(n) extra space for the built strings, though the straightforward stack-based simulation is already correct and easy to reason about.
This is a direct stack-based simulation: build each string's final "typed" result using a stack (push for regular characters, pop for "#"), then compare the two results.
Simulate typing each string independently using a stack (or equivalently, a list used as a stack), then compare the two final built strings for equality.

items: For each string, walk through its characters: push regular characters, and pop (if possible) on "#".
Join the final stack contents into a string, and compare both strings' results for equality.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A stack directly and correctly models the "type, with backspace" behavior described in the problem.
Building both final strings completely before comparing them is simple and easy to verify correct, at the cost of O(n) extra space for each built result.

blocks.text: Correctly simulates the exact typing behavior described, since a stack precisely captures "the most recently typed character gets removed by backspace."

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), where m and n are the lengths of s and t.
Space: O(m + n), for the two built result strings.

Limitation: this is already quite efficient and commonly the accepted approach; a further O(1)-extra-space variant exists (walking both strings backward from their ends, skipping backspaced characters on the fly) for interviewers specifically asking for a constant-space solution.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The stack-based approach already uses only O(n) space, but a fully O(1)-extra-space alternative exists: walk BOTH strings backward from their ends simultaneously. At each string, skip over backspaced characters on the fly (tracking a pending "skip count" for consecutive # symbols), comparing the next surviving character from each string as it is found.

For each string, maintain a pointer starting at its last index. A helper function walks that pointer backward: encountering "#" increases a skip counter and moves back; encountering a regular character while skip > 0 decrements skip and moves back (this character is cancelled); otherwise, a genuinely surviving character has been found (or the pointer went past the start). Compare the two strings' next surviving characters at each step; mismatches or one string running out before the other mean the strings are not equal.
Walk both strings backward from their ends simultaneously, skipping over backspaced characters using a running skip counter, comparing surviving characters as they are found.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Every surviving character matched between the two strings, so the result is true, matching the expected output.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), each character is visited a bounded number of times.
Space: O(1) extra, no built strings or stacks needed.

Walking backward from the end is key: a "#" encountered while walking backward always cancels the NEXT character encountered further backward (its skip count exactly tracks how many upcoming characters are cancelled), correctly reproducing what a forward stack-based simulation would have determined as "surviving," but without needing to build the full result.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A \"#\" is encountered while walking backward","The skip counter increases, and the walk continues backward past it"],["A regular character is encountered while skip > 0","It is cancelled (skip decreases), and the walk continues past it too"],["A regular character is encountered with skip == 0","It genuinely survives; this is the next character to compare"]]}

items: getNextValidIndex encapsulates the entire "skip backspaced characters" logic, callable identically for both s and t.
The main loop compares one surviving character at a time from each string, stopping early on the first mismatch (or if one string runs out of surviving characters before the other).
Both pointers are decremented by one at the end of each successful comparison, continuing the backward walk for the NEXT surviving character.

blocks.text: "Backspace" (or similar undo-the-most-recent-action) simulations are naturally modeled by a stack; when O(1) extra space is specifically required, the same logic can be replicated by walking backward and tracking a "pending cancellations" counter instead of an actual stack.

items: Popping from an empty stack when encountering "#" with nothing typed yet, rather than safely doing nothing.
In the O(1)-space version, forgetting that a single "#" can cancel MULTIPLE characters if consecutive "#"s appear (tracked correctly via the skip counter, not just a single boolean flag).
Comparing string LENGTHS after processing instead of their actual final CONTENTS, which would miss cases where two different sequences of typing happen to produce different results.

items: Starting with the straightforward stack-based simulation (easy to state and verify correct) before introducing the O(1)-space backward-walk optimization mirrors how this problem is typically expected to be solved progressively.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Simulate typing with a BACKSPACE character" points directly toward a stack (or, for O(1) space, a backward walk with a skip counter).

items: How would you solve this with O(1) extra space? Walk both strings backward from their ends, tracking a "pending cancellations" counter for consecutive "#" characters, comparing surviving characters directly without building the full result.
What if the backspace character could be customized (not always "#")? The same logic applies directly, simply checking for whatever character has been designated as the backspace symbol.

How would you handle a "select-all and delete" style operation in addition to backspace? A stack could support a "clear" operation directly (empty it entirely); the backward-walk optimization would become significantly more complex to adapt for this case.
A stack-based "undo the most recent action" simulation, conceptually related to Baseball Game elsewhere in this category, both directly modeling sequential operations with an undo/removal step.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(m + n) time, O(m + n) space.
Optimized (backward walk, skip counters): O(m + n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Stack-based typing simulation (or its O(1)-space backward-walk equivalent)
Core Idea: A regular character pushes; "#" pops (backspaces) the most recently typed character; build (or simulate) each string's final result and compare
Time: O(m + n)
Space: O(m + n) for the stack version, O(1) for the backward-walk version
Most Important Observation: "#" always cancels the MOST RECENTLY typed (not yet cancelled) character, which a stack (or a backward walk with a skip counter) captures directly
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Push regular characters, pop on "#"; compare the two final stacks
